metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the prediction of Take The Best (TTB). Because the experimental design explicitly pits TTB against Tallying (creating conflict trials where TTB points to one option and Tallying points to the other), data generated under TTB will yield a high proportion of agreement (approaching 1.0, modulo noise). Conversely, data generated under Tallying will systematically disagree with TTB on the conflict trials and guess on the tie trials, yielding an agreement score well below 0.5. The large difference in expected values ensures strong discriminability.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying heuristic. The experimental design specifically pits Tallying against Take The Best (TTB) in 5 out of the 6 trial types. On these critical trials, the highest validity cue points to one option, but a numerical majority of lower validity cues points to the other. Consequently, data generated by the Tallying theory will have a very high match rate (close to 1.0, minus noise), whereas data generated by TTB will systematically choose the opposite option, yielding a very low match rate (close to 0.16, minus noise). This produces a massive and highly reliable gap between the two theories.

In Trial 6, the options are [1, 1, 0, 0, 0] and [0, 0, 1, 1, 0]. Tallying counts exactly 2 winning features for each option, predicting a tie (exactly 50% choice probability) regardless of its beta or epsilon parameters. WADD, however, assigns a higher subjective weight to the first two features (which have higher objective validities) for any gamma > 0, leading to a systematic preference for [1, 1, 0, 0, 0]. This metric computes the proportion of times [1, 1, 0, 0, 0] is chosen in this trial type. Tallying will yield a mean of 0.5 with minimal between-subject variance (only binomial noise), while WADD will yield a mean significantly greater than 0.5.

This metric calculates the proportion of times Option A is chosen on Trials 4 and 5. In these trials, both options win on exactly two features, so Tallying predicts an exact tie (choosing A 50% of the time). However, Option A wins on higher-validity features than Option B in both cases. WADD (with any gamma > 0) will consistently assign a higher value to Option A, predicting a choice probability strictly greater than 50%.

Measures the choice probability of Option A on Trial 1. On this trial, the pure WADD model (Advocated) will predict a highly deterministic choice for Option A because the unnormalized score difference is easily scaled by its beta parameter to produce a probability close to 1.0. In contrast, the Mixture model (Competing) strictly normalizes the score difference by the sum of all weights (which is large for 8 high-validity features), shrinking the effective difference so much that even its maximum beta cannot push the choice probability as high. Additionally, Tallying predicts a tie on this trial, further anchoring the Mixture model's prediction toward 0.5.

We contrast trials where the Tallying heuristic favors Option A (Trials 6 and 7) against trials where Tallying predicts a tie (Trials 3 and 4). For the pure WADD model, the difference in weighted sums between A and B is actually larger in the tie trials than in the Tallying-favored trials at high values of the gamma parameter, meaning pure WADD will frequently predict a higher probability of choosing A in Trials 3 and 4 than in 6 and 7. In contrast, the Mixture model explicitly incorporates the Tallying heuristic, which consistently boosts the probability of choosing A in Trials 6 and 7 while diluting it toward 0.5 in Trials 3 and 4. By measuring (P(A|T6) + P(A|T7)) - (P(A|T3) + P(A|T4)), the Mixture model yields a robustly positive score, whereas the pure WADD model yields a near-zero or negative score. Combining four trials halves the binomial noise compared to a two-trial contrast, reducing between-subject variance and sharply increasing discriminability.

Under the Advocated theory (TTB + Tallying), Trial Type 1 and Trial Type 3 present the exact same heuristic conflict: TTB chooses the option with f0=1, while Tallying chooses the alternative (since 2<3 in T1 and 1<4 in T3). Because the heuristic mixture is identical, the expected difference in the probability of choosing the f0=1 option is exactly zero. Under the Competing theory (WADD + Tallying), however, the compensatory WADD strategy and the Tallying strategy both register much stronger evidence against the f0=1 option in Trial Type 3 (where it has only 1 feature vs 4) than in Trial Type 1 (where it has 2 features vs 3). Thus, the Competing model predicts a significantly positive difference.

This metric isolates trials where Tallying predicts a tie, but Take-The-Best (TTB) and Weighted Additive (WADD) predict opposite choices. On these trials, the Competing theory (a mixture of TTB and Tallying) will be entirely driven by TTB, whereas the Advocated theory (a mixture of WADD and Tallying) will be entirely driven by WADD. By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the WADD prediction on these specific trials, we expect the Advocated theory to yield values significantly above 0.5, and the Competing theory to yield values significantly below 0.5.
